extracted.intended_audience: general readers and theatre enthusiasts interested in 19th-century acting and theatrical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts practical and aesthetic criteria used in contemporary 19th‑century reviews and biography to judge an actor's performance (voice, physicality, fidelity to text, naturalness, audience effect, professional conduct). Useful for assessing period stage acting or emulating that style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / national embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor should appear as a 'palpable and obvious embodiment' of his country's spirit and habits; his biography and manner should vindicate him as 'American every inch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics praise an actor who 'is a genuine piece of the country' and whose manner and repertory grow out of his place and institutions; any slight upon him is taken as a wound directed at the country itself. Examples: Forrest seen as a creature of his institutions and daily life, striking a chord with New‑World audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical force and muscular power where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Great physical strength and muscular energy are assets for certain roles: 'It implies and demands great physical strength, a man of herculean mould.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For semi‑barbaric or physical characters (Spartacus, Polyphemus, Hercules) the material, muscular action can be the effective means of conveying the character; physical power may properly dominate intellectual subtlety in such parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of style to the character's nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor's style must suit the character: barbarian/rough characters should not be given refined, idealized treatment, and Greek/Roman heroes require different qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: it would be false to nature to depict a semi‑barbaric gladiator as if ideality governed sense; conversely, refined characters demand more delicate touches. Choose physicality or subtlety according to the role's requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and absence of stage affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting should avoid 'painted shadow', 'counterfeit manner', false readings, and 'contemptible tricks of the stage'; the performance should seem not 'acting' but identification with the role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is given when 'not one word ... is lost' and when the actor is 'free from all these defects'; deleterious effects include exaggerated declamation and theatrical gimmicks that mask the author's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional sincerity and heartfelt passion
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor must bring genuine feeling: 'He never loses sight of the belief that it is he, a man, with men before him... who asks for tears, and sobs, and answers of troubled hearts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressions should come 'from the heart rather than in the conceiving brain'; fervent, earnest delivery elicits strong audience sympathy and communal response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocal range and modulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of a 'noble voice, running from the richest base to the sweetest tenor' capable of all modulations is a key asset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voice should be flexible to produce everything from 'hurricane of savage fury to the melting tenderness of love'; vocal control aids in conveying varied emotions without resorting to artificial effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to the author's text and clarity of 'reading'
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor should preserve the poet's language: 'Not one passage—nay, not one word—of the vivid, picturesque, nervous, wondrous eloquence of the poet is lost upon the audience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective acting makes the author's meaning transparent on stage, avoiding contrived 'points' or effects that distort text; clarity of diction and understanding of authorial intent are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdued, studied finish and restraint when required
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'more subdued and quiet' style, 'readings more elaborated and studied,' and a 'dignified repose' are virtues when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress toward refinement and restraint (versus raw, overwhelming energy) is praised as maturation of performance; balance physical power with studied touches to achieve higher artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial expressiveness and subtle nonverbal communication
rubrics_metrics.description: A rare faculty of 'expressing by the face what neither pen can write nor tongue tell' is a distinguishing characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facial expression can convey nuances beyond words and is singled out by critics as a mark of exceptional acting that communicates inner life to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of stage command and quickness in stage business
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective moments include 'quick and clear directions as to the disposition of his troops' and commanding presence in stage situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond emotional effect, an actor should give precise, intelligible stage cues and direction, especially in scenes requiring control of ensemble movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the author's staging / avoidance of gratuitous stage business
rubrics_metrics.description: An actor should not introduce gratuitous or 'fancy' business that desecrates the scene or the author—such innovations can justify audience disapproval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Forrest hissed at Macready's 'fancy dance' in Hamlet as a 'desecration of the scene'; critics warn against personal mannerisms or additions that clash with the text or decorum of the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional courtesy and conduct toward colleagues
rubrics_metrics.description: Courteous, gentlemanly bearing to fellow actors is praised as important: 'no praise ... so dear to me as that which is offered by my brother actors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts of collegiality (accepting testimonials, praising and promoting others) and respectful conduct in rehearsal and company life are presented as marks of professional character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to move and sway an audience (communion with audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor should create a communal emotional effect: 'that wonderful electricity by which the inmost nature of man is moved, and masses are swayed as if by the wand of an enchanter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success is measured by moments when the house is 'hushed', when listeners are held 'from the rising to the falling of the curtain', and when applause stems from sincere, shared feeling rather than mere spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate rhetorical/declamatory style for leaders and popular speakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain characters (e.g., Jack Cade) require declamatory, trumpet‑like speech to rouse crowds rather than philosophic argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declamatory passages, even if 'too declamatory' by some standards, can be praised when they are true to the character's function as a leader who must stir 'the best sympathies of MAN'—use forceful rhetoric where historically and dramatically justified.
